Building and evaluating a function¶

Back to Functions

A Function is a formula that you write once and evaluate on any data. You describe it with an ordinary C++ callable; Pluss runs the callable a single time on placeholder variables and records the arithmetic it performs as an expression graph. After that the callable is never called again: evaluating the Function replays the recorded graph on the Series you supply, so one function serves a single point, a vector of points or a batch of grids.

A first function¶

function(variables, callable) takes the names of the variables and a callable with one Function parameter per name. The body combines those parameters with ordinary operators and the member functions listed in the next page.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace math = pluss::math;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(6));

  int traced = 0;
  const math::Function f = math::function({"x", "y"}, [&](math::Function x, math::Function y) {
    ++traced;
    return x.pow(2) * (x * y).sin();
  });

  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(0.75);

  out.writeln("arity", f.arity(), " rank", f.rank(), " variables", f.variables()[0], f.variables()[1]);
  out.writeln("by position", f({x, y}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("by name    ", f({{"y", y}, {"x", x}}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("the callable ran", traced, "time; the function was evaluated twice");
}

Output

arity 2  rank 0  variables x y
by position [0.091568, 0.681639, 3.989980]
by name     [0.091568, 0.681639, 3.989980]
the callable ran 1 time; the function was evaluated twice

The function has two variables and is a scalar formula, so its rank is 0: rank and shape describe one evaluation at scalar inputs, and evaluating on arrays adds batch dimensions in front (the next page). The two calls give identical values. The by-name form takes the arguments in any order, which is why {"y", y} can come first. The last line is the point of tracing: the callable ran once, while it was recorded, and both evaluations replayed the stored graph. Consequently the body must describe the formula with Function arithmetic. A C++ if on a placeholder cannot see any data, because during tracing there is none; write a conditional as arithmetic instead.

Binding the variables¶

A univariate Function accepts an ordinary C++ scalar directly. Use f(2.0), f(2.0F), or f(2) for a Float64, Float32, or Int64 scalar evaluation. The result is still a scalar Series, so it participates in the same platform, dtype and downstream APIs as every other evaluation. There is no need to write f({pluss::make_series(2.0)}) merely to evaluate one scalar point.

For tensor inputs or several variables, call a Function with Series values in one of two ways.

Call

Meaning

f(2.0)

one-variable scalar evaluation; float and integer overloads preserve their corresponding dtype

f({a, b})

by position: the arguments follow the order in which the variables were named

f({{"y", b}, {"x", a}})

by name, in any order; each variable exactly once

f()

for a function of no variables: evaluates the constant

Both forms also accept a RangeView of Series or of Binding (a pair<string_view, Series>), for argument lists that are built at run time. A wrong call fails with a pluss::Error that names the problem. The program below makes each mistake once and prints the first line of the message.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

#include <functional>
#include <string>

namespace math = pluss::math;
using namespace pluss::tils;

// The first line of an error message (the rest says where it was raised).
static std::string head(const char *what) {
  const std::string text(what);
  return text.substr(0, text.find('\n'));
}

static void attempt(OutputEngine &out, const char *label, const std::function<void()> &call) {
  try {
    call();
    out.writeln(label, "-> accepted");
  } catch (const pluss::Error &e) {
    out.writeln(label, "->", head(e.what()));
  }
}

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  const math::Function f = math::function({"x", "y"}, [](math::Function x, math::Function y) { return x * y + 1.0; });
  const auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});

  attempt(out, "no arguments:        ", [&] { (void)f(); });
  attempt(out, "one of two, by name: ", [&] { (void)f({{"x", a}}); });
  attempt(out, "unknown name:        ", [&] { (void)f({{"x", a}, {"z", a}}); });
  attempt(out, "name given twice:    ", [&] { (void)f({{"x", a}, {"x", a}, {"y", a}}); });
  attempt(out, "one of two, by order:", [&] { (void)f({a}); });
  attempt(out, "undefined Series:    ", [&] { (void)f({a, pluss::Series{}}); });
  attempt(out, "correct call:        ", [&] { (void)f({a, a}); });
}

Output

no arguments:         -> math::Function: ordered argument count 0 does not match function arity 2
one of two, by name:  -> math::Function: missing variable binding 'y'
unknown name:         -> math::Function: unknown variable binding 'z'
name given twice:     -> math::Function: duplicate variable binding 'x'
one of two, by order: -> math::Function: ordered argument count 1 does not match function arity 2
undefined Series:     -> math::Function: arguments must be defined Series values
correct call:         -> accepted

Every failure is a pluss::Error raised at the call, before any arithmetic happens, and the message names the offending variable or the two counts. Evaluate with exactly the declared variables, once each. A by-name call may list them in any order; a by-position call must list all of them.

Which callables are accepted¶

The callable can be anything with a fixed number of Function parameters: a lambda, a function pointer, a function object, a std::function, or an object that owns move-only state. It must return a Function, a Series or an arithmetic scalar; a Series or scalar result becomes a constant. The number of parameters has to equal the number of names.

When the number of variables is only known at run time, take a single std::span<const Function> instead. The names can then come from any range of strings, and the function can have as many variables as the data requires.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

#include <functional>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace math = pluss::math;
using namespace pluss::tils;

math::Function blend(math::Function a, math::Function b) { return a * 0.25 + b * 0.75; }

struct Square {
  math::Function operator()(math::Function v) const { return v * v; }
};

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const auto t = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 4.0});

  const math::Function from_lambda = math::function({"t"}, [](math::Function v) { return v + 1.0; });
  const math::Function from_pointer = math::function({"a", "b"}, &blend);
  const math::Function from_object = math::function({"t"}, Square{});
  const std::function<math::Function(math::Function)> erased = [](math::Function v) { return v.exp(); };
  const math::Function from_std_function = math::function({"t"}, erased);

  out.writeln("lambda       ", from_lambda({t}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("pointer      ", from_pointer({t, t}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("object       ", from_object({t}).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("std::function", from_std_function({t}).pull<double>());

  // Names held in a std::vector<std::string>, and a sum over however many variables there are.
  std::vector<std::string> names;
  for (int i = 0; i < 6; ++i) names.push_back("v" + std::to_string(i));
  const math::Function total = math::function(names, [](std::span<const math::Function> v) {
    math::Function sum = v[0];
    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < v.size(); ++i) sum = sum + v[i];
    return sum;
  });
  std::vector<pluss::Series> args(6, t);
  out.writeln("arity", total.arity(), " sum of six copies of t", total(pluss::RangeView<pluss::Series>(args)).pull<double>());
}

Output

lambda        [2.0000, 3.0000, 5.0000]
pointer       [1.0000, 2.0000, 4.0000]
object        [1.0000, 4.0000, 16.0000]
std::function [2.7183, 7.3891, 54.5982]
arity 6  sum of six copies of t [6.0000, 12.0000, 24.0000]

All four forms trace identically. The from_pointer function has two variables (a and b) and was evaluated with t for both, so it returns 0.25 t + 0.75 t = t. The span form is how to build a function whose number of variables is a run-time quantity: the six names come from a std::vector<std::string> and the body folds however many placeholders it receives. Its argument list is likewise a RangeView<Series> built from a vector. The names are copied when the function is created, so the vector may be destroyed afterwards.

Rules for the variable list¶

  • Each name must be non-empty and appear once.

  • The number of names must equal the callable’s number of parameters (for a fixed-parameter callable).

  • The callable must return something: an undefined Function is rejected.

  • A Function obtained from one function(...) call cannot be returned from the body of another; each call starts its own set of placeholders.

The next page lists everything the body may do with a placeholder.
